He does make a point about some people just wanting to complain, and that's good if you can filter out the noise. But some feedback is valuable and if you discount all of it as people just beating their chest then I think that's pretty short sighted.

He has a point about the amount of data they can derive from a game, most of it is possible because of the draconian drm and what not but i digress on that point. The thing is though, that data is rather meaningless, just because I pick the quest to find the golden duck over the quest to slay the dragon doesnt tell you anything about me. I seriously doubt the truthfulness of the assertion that the biggest complainers in their forums are the biggest spenders, he says so him self, "people lie, like a lot."

Well, it's not hard (like it's 0% conjecture for EA) for them to look at a forum account which had to be tied to a game account, and see how much the game account has spent. I wouldn't really challenge that assertion, especially since he's making it in a small forum and likely wasn't trying to play some PR angle.

On the flip side, I see a lot of hubris in his statement that telemetry rules all. Too often in the tech development world, user telemetry is worshipped like a god and actual user feedback is ignored. I've participated in more than one beta, in fact, where I received feedback that my opinion or feedback wasn't particularly valid because I was using the product in a way most consumers don't.

The huge problem with an approach like this, and with Rich's approach, is that pleasing the majority actually isn't always the best way to make the most money. Maybe in gaming it is, that's not really a field I work in, but in many other markets, the vocal minority can really make or break your product. When it comes to most technological items, for example, the majority of my family just asks me what they should buy, and they go with that. If I make a recommendation based on my opinion of a product, suddenly my "not normal use" dissatisfaction becomes a bunch of lost sales. And I'm not particularly influential, just friends & family...

In any case, maybe your biggest payers complain the most, but all that tells you is that they've paid in the past. I would worry about how to secure your future revenue stream and if your actions are building towards that or burning away at the goodwill you've built.

In my experience the biggest complainers are the ones that are trying to find a way to stick with the thing they are complaining about despite the complaints. When your voice isnt heard after that... you often realize that it wont be heard and then leave. To be honest it doesnt matter who he was talking to, he had to have known it would eventually become public, any intelligent business man will know to tailor his words for the public despite the current audience.
